title: What Battle Cards is now
subtitle: Twelve years of building in deep tech. Why I treat it like a playground. And why I write everything down, so the people around me make new mistakes instead of my old ones.

content.text: In January 2021 I wrote a line I still think about.
If any of your friends tell you they are going to build a deep tech startup, the biggest favour you can do is to shoot them while they are still happy.

It was a joke. Mostly. I had just come out the other side of Scapic, a no-code platform for augmented and virtual reality, which Flipkart had acquired a few weeks before. I was tired, proud and a little stunned that it had worked at all.
Then I kept building deep tech anyway. Spatial tools. A creative tech studio. Smart glasses. And now AI. Five more years of exactly the thing I told my friends to avoid.

So this is the long version of why. It is about building at the frontier when nobody, including you, knows how the story ends. It is about treating that uncertainty like a playground instead of a war. And it is about what Battle Cards has become: small, tactical guides I write so the people around me can see what I see, move faster, and make new mistakes instead of repeating mine.
If a friend tells you they are building deep tech, don't shoot them. Send them this.
Deep Tech Is Mostly Fog
Start with what makes deep tech different, because it is not just harder software.

When you build a normal software product, most of the risk is market risk. Can you build a to-do app? Of course you can. The question is whether anyone wants yours, and whether you can reach them. That is hard, but the technology itself is not in doubt.

Deep tech stacks a second risk on top. You do not know if the thing can be built. Or built cheaply enough. Or built in time. Then, once it works, you still face the market question, and it is worse than usual, because you are often selling something people have never seen.
I find it useful to draw this as a simple 2x2.

Across the bottom is market risk: do people want it? Up the side is technology risk: can it be built? Most software lives with an easy build and uncertain demand. Research labs live with a hard build and demand assumed. Deep tech startups live in the corner where both questions are open at once, and each one makes the other harder to answer.
That corner has a texture that is hard to describe until you have lived there. The closest word I have is fog.

In the fog, plans stop working. You can write a beautiful eighteen-month roadmap and watch one hardware delay, one model release or one platform change turn it into fiction by month three. Timelines stretch. The thing you were sure was the hard part turns out easy, and the thing you thought was a detail eats a year.

The usual startup advice was written for clearer weather. Talk to users, ship fast, find product market fit. All true. But in the fog you often cannot ship the real thing fast, and users cannot tell you what they want from a technology they have never touched. You walk forward with a flashlight, leave breadcrumbs, and hope the lighthouse is roughly where you think it is.
Over twelve years I have come to believe there are two ways to work in that fog. You can treat it as a war: grit, burn, endure, wait for the exit. Or you can treat it as a playground.
I have tried both. The playground wins.
Chapter One: The Dorm Room
I started trying to make things during my engineering undergrad. Most of them did not work. A few did.

The first real one was Aeriem, an adaptive learning platform for K-12 schools. The second was Supertext, hyperlocal delivery that ran on WhatsApp, long before that was a normal thing to do. I sold my first startup while I was still in college, which taught me something useful and something dangerous at the same time.

The useful thing was that building is a skill, and skills compound. Each attempt, even the ones that went nowhere, made the next one faster. You learn how to talk to a customer, how to cut scope, how to write the email that gets a reply.
The dangerous thing was that an early win makes you believe the outcome is the point. It is not. The outcome is mostly weather. What you control is the shape of your trying.

Looking back, the dorm room years were already a playground. I just did not have the word for it yet. We built because building was fun, because the tools were in front of us, and because it beat the alternative. Nobody had told us how hard it was supposed to be, which was a gift.
Chapter Two: Scapic, the Toy
Scapic was where I learned what deep tech actually feels like.

The idea was simple to say and hard to do: the simplest way to create, share and explore augmented reality, virtual reality and 3D experiences, with no code. We called it Scapic mostly because the domain was available. It ended up being a word everyone spelled wrong. It still got acquired.

At the time, a lot of people looked at AR and VR and saw a toy. Headsets were clunky. Phone AR was jittery. The use cases were demos. And they were right, the way people are always right about the early version of something.

But I had come to believe something I later wrote on one of the first battle cards: the next big thing starts as a toy, before it disrupts an industry. People play with things long before they pay for them. When someone dismisses a thing as just a toy, that is often the most useful signal you get all month.

So we built the toy, seriously. Hundreds of thousands of experiences were made on Scapic. It became, at the time, the largest AR commerce platform in India. Brands used it so you could place a sofa in your living room, or see a sneaker before you bought it.
Towards the end of 2020, Flipkart acquired Scapic. The mission we had written for ourselves, bringing augmented reality to a billion Indians, suddenly had a much bigger engine behind it.

The lesson I took from Scapic is the one I most want to hand to anyone starting in deep tech. You do not win by being certain. You win by being early to the toy, staying in the room long enough for it to grow up, and enjoying the room while you wait.
Chapter Three: Inside the Giant

After the acquisition, I spent some years inside Flipkart, building and scaling camera and Labs work across AR commerce and emerging technology. Labs, in practice, meant seeding deep tech bets inside one of the largest commerce companies in the country.
It is a strange and educational place to be: a small, weird team inside a very large, very sensible machine.

What surprised me was this. The fog does not lift because you are big. A large company has more money, more data and more distribution, and all of those help. But the core questions in deep tech, can it be built and does anyone want it, are just as open inside a giant as in a garage. What changes is the cost of being wrong. In a startup, a wrong bet costs you a quarter. Inside a large company, it can cost you your credibility, so people start to bet less.
That is the quiet tax on innovation inside big companies. Not a lack of talent. A lack of play.

The Labs work that went well, in my experience, had playground rules. Small bets with clear edges. A fast way to kill what was not working. Prototypes people could touch, because a demo you can hold changes minds in a way a slide never does. And a team that enjoyed the experiments, because enjoyment is what kept them trying after the third failure.
Chapter Four: Many Small Playgrounds

After Flipkart, I did something that looked chaotic from the outside and felt natural from the inside. I built several things at once, each one a different playground at the edge of what was possible.

Reality Tools built spatial and immersive tooling, and was later acquired by MotionPage. Cope.Studio was a creative technology studio, building product, brand and web3 experiments, and was later acquired by Polygon. Dehidden was acquired by Layer-E. Along the way the patents piled up; there are now more than fifteen of them in deep tech.

I want to be careful not to make this sound like a plan. It was not one. It was closer to a portfolio of experiments, each small enough to start quickly, each at the frontier of something I found genuinely interesting, and each teaching me something the others could use.

This is the part of the playground idea that gets misunderstood. A playground is not a lack of seriousness. Children on a playground are deeply serious about the game. A playground is a space with soft edges, where falling is expected and cheap, where you can try the big slide, and where the point is to keep playing rather than to win once.

In deep tech, that framing does something useful. It turns exits into chapters instead of finish lines. Starting, failing, scaling, learning, exiting, and then the slightly empty question: now what? If the exit is the only part you enjoy, you have enjoyed one day out of two thousand. If the work itself is the playground, you get to enjoy all of them.
Chapter Five: Glasses

Smart glasses are the deepest deep tech I have touched, because every hard problem meets there at once. Optics. Batteries. Heat. Weight. Privacy. Social acceptance. And now AI, which finally gives glasses something worth doing.

SeeIt began as an open-source AI smart glasses research lab. The question that pulled me in was simple: what happens when the computer can see what you see, and remember it? The answer we keep coming back to fits in one line: any glasses, any AI, one memory.

Hardware is humbling in a way software never is. You cannot push a fix overnight to a hinge. A sample takes weeks to arrive. The render always looks better than the thing in your hand. Every lesson from the fog applies twice.

It is also the most fun I have had in years. Nothing beats putting on a pair of glasses you helped build and watching them understand a room. That feeling is the whole reason to live in the foggy corner. You do not get it anywhere else.
Why a Playground, Not a War
Let me pull the thread together, because the playground idea is more than a mood. It is a practical operating system for uncertain work.

The war framing says deep tech is a long grind toward a distant victory. Endure the pain, and the exit pays for it. I understand why founders adopt it; the work genuinely is hard. But it has three problems.
First, it makes you rigid. Wars have plans, and plans are exactly what the fog destroys. A founder in war mode keeps marching toward the original objective long after the terrain has changed.

Second, it burns people out. You can sustain a sprint on adrenaline. You cannot sustain ten years on it. The deep tech timeline is long, and the people who last are the ones who find the daily work itself rewarding.

Third, and most important, it makes you hoard. In a war, information is power, and power gets concentrated. The founder holds the map. Everyone else follows orders. That works when the map is right. In the fog, the map is never fully right, and the person holding it cannot see everything.
The playground framing fixes all three.

A playground is built for exploration. You are supposed to try the slide, the swings and the climbing frame, and you are supposed to fall off a few of them. That maps neatly onto how deep tech actually moves: lots of cheap exploration, then a commitment once something works.
A playground has edges. Good ones are fenced, with soft ground. In practice that means small bets with clear boundaries, so a failure costs a week, not a company.
And a playground is shared. Nobody plays alone for long. Which brings me to the part I care about most.
Playground Rules
If the playground is the operating system, these are its rules. None of them are clever. All of them were learned by breaking them first.
Fence the playground.

Every experiment gets an edge before it starts: a time box, a budget, a question it is meant to answer. Deep tech experiments love to grow without limit, because there is always one more thing to try. The fence is what makes falling cheap. When you hit it, you stop, look at what you learned, and decide whether to build a bigger playground next door.
Make it touchable early.

A rough thing someone can hold beats a polished thing they can only imagine. With Scapic, the moment that changed minds was always the same: a sofa appearing in someone's own living room, on their own phone. No slide ever did that. In hardware the rule is even stronger. Get a sample into a hand, because the hand will tell you things the render never will.
Cheap first, expensive last.

Ideas cost nothing, so explore them freely. Prototypes cost a little, so explore a few. Real manufacturing, real launches and real hires cost the most, so save them for the winners. Most deep tech companies that die, in my experience, spent expensive money on a question cheap money could have answered.
Keep two clocks.

One clock runs on weeks: what did we learn this week? The other runs on years: is the technology moving toward us or away? Founders who only watch the short clock get busy and lost. Founders who only watch the long one get grand and broke. You need both on the wall.
Kill things kindly.

In a playground, leaving the swings to try the slide is not failure; it is the point. Teams that are punished for stopping experiments will never stop them, and you will end up with a graveyard of zombie projects. Celebrate a clean kill. Write down why. Then move on.
Enjoy the climb, on purpose.

This sounds soft. It is not. Enjoyment is fuel, and deep tech runs for a decade. If you do not deliberately make the work fun, the fog will make it miserable for you. Pick problems that delight you. Work with people you like. Celebrate the small wins, because the big one may be years away.
The Archive
Battle Cards started from a simple equation I wrote down years ago.
Startups are speed of execution. Faster execution means more chances of mistakes. To avoid the mistakes, read and learn.

The trouble, which I noticed quickly, is that reading more is not the same as getting better. You can finish a book a week and repeat the same mistake every quarter, because the lesson never made it from the page into a habit.

So I started writing down the lessons I found useful, in a format small enough to actually use. I called them screenshot-sized essays: one idea, sized to fit on a phone screen, built to be saved and acted on. Over time they became battle cards.

I now keep an archive of them. When I counted earlier this year, there were 1,576 entries across six years and five companies. Most are just titles now, and the titles are the interesting part, because they show what I kept coming back to. Asymmetric bets on people. The founder is a shock absorber. Taste vs skill. Hard startups. The painful path. Enter after the peak.
Different companies, different technology, same questions. That is what an archive teaches you that memory cannot: the same handful of problems show up again and again, wearing different clothes.
Context Is the Thing You Share
Now the core idea of this whole piece, plainly.

In deep tech, the scarcest thing is not money or talent. It is context. Why we chose this approach. What we already tried. Which supplier missed the lead time. Which demo actually changed the customer's mind. What the last failure felt like from the inside.
Most of that context lives in the founder's head. A team without it will do the only rational thing: rediscover it, by making the same mistakes the founder already made.

That is the most expensive kind of mistake there is. An old mistake teaches you nothing new. It just costs time you will not get back. A new mistake is different. A new mistake is tuition. It means the team is out at the edge of the playground, where nobody has been, learning something that did not exist before.
So the goal of a deep tech team is not to avoid mistakes. That is impossible in the fog. The goal is to stop making old ones, so all your mistakes are new.
The way you do that is by sharing context, constantly, in a form people will actually absorb.

That is what battle cards are for now. They are not motivational quotes. They are compressed context. Each one says: this is a thing I learned the hard way, this is why it holds up, and this is how to use it this week. I hand them to my team. I use them on myself. They are the closest thing I have found to installing a lesson in someone else's head without making them pay for it first.

There is a second-order effect I did not expect. When everyone shares the same context, the team moves faster even when I am not in the room. People make calls I would have made, for the reasons I would have made them, and then they push past me into territory I have not seen. That is when a team starts compounding.

In practice, the sharing has a few simple rituals. A new person on the team gets a starter pack of cards before their first week, so they meet the old mistakes on paper instead of in production. After anything goes wrong, someone writes the card within the week, and it goes to everyone who might hit the same wall. When a card stops being true, it gets marked and retired in the open, so people learn that the archive is alive. And when a teammate writes a card I would never have written, that is the best day of the month, because it means the context is now flowing in both directions.

None of this needs software. A shared folder and a habit will do. What it needs is a founder who believes that giving away what they know makes the team stronger, not the founder weaker. In the fog, it always does.
The People Around You
Sharing context is the big idea. But there is a quieter version of it that applies to the founder too, and I learned it the hard way, in the months after Scapic was acquired.

When you build in the fog for long enough, it is scarily easy to feel directionless and stop trusting your own voice. Plateauing is normal. Staying there is the problem. In early 2021 I wrote about the habits that pulled me out, and they have aged better than almost anything else I wrote that year.
Get out of the building.
Whatever you are working on, stop confining it to the walls of your room. Meet peers, and better, leaders. Watch how they run their days and their teams. Steal one habit at a time.
Collect traits, not heroes.
Role models are a trap, because nobody is great at everything and copying a whole person copies their flaws too. Keep an eye out for individual traits instead, and practise them in your own voice.
Appoint a personal board.
You need a few people who root for you in specific parts of your life. Do not ask them for answers. Ask them how they would think about the problem. You want better questions, not borrowed decisions.
Draw a map.

Reflection is scary when it is vague. A map makes it concrete. Mine has three axes: scope, from project to team to company; people versus product; and the last six months versus the next six. Then you mark it up. Heart the work you loved. Star what your teammates say you are uniquely good at. Cross out what drains you, and find someone who loves it.

Every one of these is really the same move as the battle cards. It is context, shared on purpose. With yourself, with a few people you trust, with the people you work beside. The fog is thinner when there are more flashlights.
The Half-Life of a Lesson
There is a catch, and it is especially sharp right now.

Lessons decay. In a piece I wrote earlier this year, I described how every role now has a half-life: the time between learning a method and watching that method lose part of its value. It used to run in years. In AI work it can feel closer to six months.

The craft rarely disappears. The method changes. A photographer still needs composition, light and taste, even when the node graph they built gets replaced by a model that edits through conversation. An engineer still needs systems thinking, even when an agent writes the first draft.

That means an archive of lessons is not a museum. It is a garden. Some cards stay true for a decade: the toy becomes the industry, the idea eats the founder, get out of the building. Others expire in a season and should be retired without guilt. Part of the job is pruning.
The cards that last tend to be about people and judgement. The cards that expire tend to be about tools. That alone is a useful lesson.
The Playground Got Bigger
One more chapter, because it changes how all of this feels right now.

For most of my career, deep tech meant years of slow, expensive exploration before you knew whether you had anything. AI has quietly changed that. A model can explore more shapes before lunch than a studio could in a month. A small team can prototype in an afternoon what used to need a quarter. The fog is still there, but you can send many more flashlights into it at once, and they are cheaper than they have ever been.

That is wonderful, and it is also a trap. When exploring gets cheap, it becomes very easy to explore forever and never commit. The playground fills up with half-built slides. The skill that matters most now is the one that was always hardest: judgement. Knowing which of the two hundred things you tried is the one worth building. Knowing when to stop playing on the swings and start building the bridge.

Judgement is also the thing that transfers worst. You cannot hand someone your taste in a meeting. But you can hand them the reasons behind it, one small card at a time, until their judgement starts to rhyme with yours, and then improve on it. That, more than anything, is why I keep writing these.
How I Write a Battle Card
If you want to try this with your own team, this is the method, stripped down.
One idea per card.
If you need a paragraph to explain it, you have two cards.
Three parts, always.
What the idea is. Why it holds up. How to use it this week. Nothing else.
Write it the week it happens.
Lessons rot fast. The week after a failure, you remember exactly what it felt like and why it happened. A month later, you remember a tidy story.
Make it screenshot-sized.
If it does not fit on one phone screen, nobody will read it twice.
Show the idea, do not just say it.
Every card gets a picture of the idea next to the words. People remember the picture long after the sentence.
Hand it to one person.
A card nobody receives is a diary entry. The point is transfer.
Retire cards that stop being true.
An archive full of expired advice is worse than no archive.
Why Foldables Are the Perfect Format
A small confession. I have started reading battle cards on a foldable phone, and it has changed how I make them.

A foldable gives you two screens side by side. It turns out that is exactly the right shape for a battle card. The left screen holds the insight: what, why and how. The right screen holds the visual: a picture of the idea that makes it stick. You read the words with one eye and see the idea with the other.

Screenshot-sized essays were already built for phones. On a foldable they get genuinely fun to consume. They stop feeling like text and start feeling like objects. Open the phone, and the card opens with it, the way a book does.
So from now on, every battle card on this Substack comes in that shape: the insight on the left, the visual on the right, as if you were holding it open in your hands.
A Letter to the Dorm Room

If I could slide one card under the door of the dorm room where all of this started, it would not be about technology. It would be a short list. These are the things I wish someone had told me before the first startup, and that I now try to tell every new person who joins a team of mine.
The outcome is weather. The trying is yours.
You will have wins you did not deserve and losses you did not earn. Judge yourself on the quality of your attempts, not the scoreboard on a given day.
Be early to the toy.
The things worth building at the frontier usually look silly at first. If serious people are laughing a little, you might be in the right place. If everyone already agrees, you are probably late.
Hold the plan loosely and the purpose tightly.
The roadmap will change every quarter. The reason you are building should not. When those two get confused, teams either thrash or freeze.
Write it down while it hurts.
The most valuable lesson from a failure is available for about a week. After that, your brain rewrites the story to protect you. Catch it before it does.
Share more than feels comfortable.

Founders tend to under-share, because explaining takes time and it feels faster to just decide. It is faster this week. It is much slower this year, because every decision then has to route through you.
Old mistakes are a tax. New mistakes are tuition.
Pay as little tax as you can. Spend freely on tuition.
Pick people you would happily be stuck in the fog with.
Deep tech means long stretches without good news. The people beside you are the weather you can actually choose.
Enjoy it.
Not as a reward at the end. As the method. The fun is what keeps you curious, and curiosity is what finds the way through.
None of these are original. Most are things I read and nodded at long before I actually understood them. That gap, between nodding at a lesson and living it, is the whole reason battle cards exist.
What Battle Cards Is Now
Battle Cards started in 2020 as a newsletter about building deep tech products, written in the gap after Scapic. Six years later, it is a few things at once.

It is a stash of tactical cards: small guides I write for my team and for myself, sized for a phone and shaped for a foldable. Each one is a piece of context I would rather share than let someone rediscover the hard way.
It is a place for long essays on how technology is changing creative work, written slowly, with the diagrams I scribble while thinking.

And it is a playground. A place to try the most audacious crossroads I can find between the creative world and the technology world, run experiments in the open, and share what comes back: what worked, what broke, and the files behind it.

If you are building in deep tech, the honest advice has not changed much since 2021. It is uncertain. It is slow. It will humble you. But you get to choose how you hold it. Hold it like a war and it will grind you down. Hold it like a playground, and share the map with everyone on it, and something better happens. You enjoy the climb. Your team moves faster. And every mistake you make is a new one.
